en: The Ritual Manual for the Recitation of the Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva’s Cintāmaṇicakra Dhāraṇī, with Preface.
Spoken by the Sui Dynasty Patriarch Zhiyi. Based on the four types of samādhi, [the Patriarch] demonstrated the practice methods of various sūtras.
Although many have read them, few have practiced them. Why is this so? Because of people...
Their faculties are shallow and the flavor of the Dharma is diluted;
they labor under their teachers over mere names and forms,
and are remiss in serving the Buddha through the cultivation of merit.
Consequently, the Ten Contemplations as a complete vehicle and the Five Repentances as auxiliary practices have become nothing more than empty words.
During my leisure time from lecturing and studying, I felt this keenly.
Diligently seeking the benefits of reciting mantras,
he opened the scripture repository and obtained four copies of the *Cintāmaṇicakra-dhāraṇī*.

Examining its text, it is clearly the same work translated differently. One version was by Śikṣānanda (translated as "Awakening Joy" in Chinese), translated during the first year of the Jiǔshì era under Empress Wu of the Tang dynasty;
it consists of eight sheets.
Second, the *Amītyanā*, translated during the second year of the Shenglong era of the Zhongzong reign;
this title means "Jewel Contemplation" (*Ratnacintā*).
Seven sheets.
Translated during the reign of Empress Wu of the Tang dynasty by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing.
Three pages.
Fourth: the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Tang dynasty.
This was translated by Jue’ai.
With its nineteen folios, the text is concise in its phrasing and its method is succinct;
it can suppress evil and thereby exhaust the three obstacles.

One who upholds the good can fulfill the two adornments. The Dharma Master from India in the Western Regions, whose name was Zunshe, constantly contemplated this sutra and understood its essential means for benefiting sentient beings.
He particularly cherished the incantations translated by Yijing because they were easy to recite; he therefore carved them onto wooden printing blocks and distributed them to the fourfold assembly.
However, Jing’s translation is somewhat abbreviated regarding the ritual procedures for the recitation; it merely states that one should collect the mind and recite orally.
As for the specific rites and visualizations, these have never been indicated.
Consequently, at the time of receiving and upholding [the practice], the practitioner's intention may be deficient as it is now.
I have gathered from various texts to provide supplementary material.
From the beginning to the end, these are organized into seven sections in total.
First: Ritual Procedures (*vidhi*).
Second, visualization;
third, prostration and praise;
fourth, recitation.
Five: Repentance and Vows;
Six: Testimonies and Verification;
Seven: Dispelling Doubts.
All of these follow the precedent of the original scripture so that the source and its stream are not separated.
Thus, the ancient regulations value the continuity of the "basket and fur" (the legacy of one's ancestors).
I acknowledge my own faults and await future sages.
The First Ritual Procedure. The Sūtra says:
"If there are good sons or good daughters, bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs..."
Upāsakas and upāsikās who resolve to seek the rewards of this life in the present should single-mindedly receive and uphold this mantra.
When wishing to receive and uphold [this teaching],
one need not inquire about the auspiciousness of the sun, moon, or stars, nor perform separate observances of fasting and precepts;
furthermore, it does not require ritual bathing or clean robes.
Simply by ceasing all else and concentrating the mind to recite it orally without slackening,
hundreds of thousands of kinds of undertakings and aspirations will all be fulfilled.
There is no other mantra more efficacious than this King of Wish-Fulfilling Mantras.
Regarding those of equal power:
if one recites [the mantra] one hundred and eight times every day,
one will immediately behold Avalokiteśvara and the others.
The number of recitations translated by Śikṣānanda is likewise the same.
It continues uninterruptedly for seven days and seven nights. Jinadharma’s translation states:
"One should recite it one thousand and eight times during the final watch of the night or at dawn."
Up until the final watch of every day, one should recite it three thousand times.
Liu Zhi’s translation states:
"One should regularly recite it one thousand and eighty times at the fifth watch."
Furthermore, it is said that one should recite one thousand and eighty times during each of the six periods of the day, continuing without interruption;
for each individual syllable, one should complete three lakṣas (one lakṣa being a term in the Sanskrit language).
This is called the "Ten Thousand Recitations. Furthermore, it is said:
if a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī recites one hundred and eight times, if a man recites one hundred and six times, and if a woman recites one hundred and three times.
If a young boy recites it one hundred times,
or if a young girl recites it ninety times,
this is called the method of daily practice (*kai-hō*).
All supreme matters shall achieve fulfillment for kings, queens, princesses, and high officials.
Regarding the four castes—each having its own specific number—I shall now attempt to discuss them.
Now, as for the language of the Western Brahmans,
it has been transmitted differently across the five regions of India; consequently, the translations made in China differ from one another,
such that the fundamental texts revered by the masters of the Tripitaka are not the same.
This matter rests solely upon the judgment of the sages and is difficult to fathom through mere sentiment;
therefore, we shall correctly employ the original text of Yijing and request that one hundred and eight recitations be taken as the standard. The reason for this is as follows:
This is to manifest the destruction of the one hundred and eight afflictions and to achieve the one hundred and eight samādhis.
Furthermore, Yi Jing stated:
If one recites it once through,
all the aforementioned matters will be fulfilled according to one's wishes.
Furthermore, Baosiwei’s translation states:
When receiving and upholding [this], there is no need for arduous effort; simply reciting it will bring success.
Speaking from this perspective:
Even if one does not reach one hundred and eight recitations,
there should be no fault in reducing the number according to the count.
The time periods for recitation differ across various editions.
This is because it depends on the differences in the faculties and inclinations of individuals.
Now, it is said that if one recites based on the practice of seven days and seven nights,
one must perform one hundred and eight recitations during each of the six periods of the day and night.
This is like the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra*, which limits [the period] to twenty-one days,
or the invitation to Avalokiteśvara, which limits it to forty-nine days, and so forth.
If one recites it every day at the fifth watch of the night, just before dawn:
This constitutes the regular practice;
there is no fixed number for it.
If one were to say otherwise, it would not be so.
How can one fulfill three lakṣas?
Could such a vast number be achieved within seven days?
Furthermore, if it does not reach the time of the fifth watch or dawn, [how could it be accomplished?]
This is also according to one's own preference.
It is designated as "the latter part of the night" (yāma) because it is used for interrogation;
it is mentioned separately because at dawn the human mind is clear and refreshed.
The reason for Jing’s translation was to accommodate the leniency of the times.
According to the version by Zhu Faliu,
one should now dwell in a quiet chamber during the day and night.
Facing east and sitting cross-legged, one should visualize the Holy Avalokiteśvara as being present before one's eyes; reciting his name without distraction,
one should burn aloeswood incense, offer mental worship, and pay reverent homage.
One should provide offerings of incense and flowers according to what one can afford, without interruption.
It should be understood that prior to reciting the mantra,
one must withdraw the mind in a quiet room and engage in visualization.
Next, enter the maṇḍala and perform prostrations and offerings.
The images set out must face directly west.
Furthermore, do not construct an altar; simply spread out seats and cushions.
It is arranged in three tiers; on the upper tier, the Dharma Jewel is placed, which is the dhāraṇī that is upheld.
To the left of the scripture, an image of Śākyamuni is installed, and to the right, an image of Amitābha is installed.
The middle tier features only an image of Avalokiteśvara in the posture of peaceful meditation,
with either flowers or lamps on its left and right;
the lower tier consists solely of a row of offering implements.
If one is unable to arrange it as described above, one may simply follow the conventional format of a ritual site;

or, maintaining only an image of the Bodhisattva, provide offerings according to one's means. Although it is said that bathing and pure garments are not required in such cases, [one should still act with care].
It is especially beneficial to practice separately for seven days.
Thus, Jue-xi translated it as follows:
"If one desires that the Noble Avalokiteśvara manifest as a boon-granting deity..."
Having bathed for purification, rubbed the body with incense, and put on clean garments,
one should perform the extensive offerings as detailed in that sutra, including the invitation, reception, and dismissal [of the deity].
All [versions] include the mudrās and mantras;
however, these are missing from other editions and are no longer practiced today.
Contemplation and Visualization, Part Two: Now, sentient beings since beginningless time have been hindered by dullness and distraction, which obstruct their luminosity and stillness.
Consequently, while worldly afflictions externally enslave them, the wisdom of the Path is internally blind.

The realities of the eight sufferings press upon them without ceasing, and the marks of the two adornments remain impoverished and unattained. Thus, they drift through accumulated kalpas, solitary and exposed, yet lacking self-reflection.
It is solely what the mind brings forth;
the Sages, taking pity on sentient beings,
provisionally employ esoteric language to expound the subtle and wondrous Dharma.
Instruct them to receive and uphold [the teachings].
First, provide for their worldly happiness;
next, restore their Tathāgata-nature.
He exhorted them repeatedly, as a wasp charms a caterpillar.
Is it not swift for one who not only recites with the mouth but further contemplates with the mind?
Liu Zhi translated this as follows:
If one truly accomplishes this most supreme dharani-method,
then in all circumstances— whether eating or not eating, whether pure or impure—
one should with single-minded focus visualize the holy Avalokiteśvara, his marks and signs complete, radiant and brilliant like the rising sun.
By reciting this dhāraṇī, one will be free from deluded thoughts;
by constantly maintaining it without interruption and without a single transgression,
one shall attain the manifestation of the Bodhisattva’s golden-hued body.
Having removed all obstructive defilements through the empowerment of spiritual power, whatever aspirations the mind seeks shall be entirely fulfilled.
Zhen Na’s translation states:
"When reciting and contemplating, one should keep in mind Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva and seek him as a refuge."

Thus, when mind and speech correspond and recitation and visualization are practiced in unison, the mastery of upholding [the mantra] is perfected; however, for a beginner whose mind is distracted, it is difficult to collect it.
Therefore, sitting cross-legged in a quiet room, one should first contemplate the sacred form.
Since the scriptural text is concise, I shall now assist in elucidating it.

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva’s fundamental realization of wondrous enlightenment is titled "Righteous Dharma Radiance" (Zhengfaming), while his provisional manifestation in the position of the successor to Buddhahood is named "Avalokiteśvara. Although the fundamental and the provisional differ, [they are one].
There is nothing that does not arise as the function of responsive transformation following the essence of True Suchness (tathatā).
Its essence is like a mirror; its function is like a reflected image.
Therefore, the Truth itself does not respond; the response resides in the capacity of the recipient.
It is just as a mirror does not itself take on an image; rather, the image exists according to the form [that presents it].
Furthermore, since capacities have degrees of superiority and inferiority, the manifestations [of the Buddha] must vary in scale.

The greatest manifestation has a body eighty thousand billion nayutas of yojanas in height, as described in the *Sixteen Contemplations Sutra*. The smallest manifestation appears in all places with a body identical to that of sentient beings.
The Great Response manifests in the Land of Ultimate Bliss,
while the Lesser Response wanders through all defiled lands.
As the Sūtra says:
The Potalaka Mountain where Bodhisattvas dwell is precisely the place shown for wandering and staying within this land;
now, one should newly resolve to cultivate contemplation.
If one’s mental faculty is weak, one should practice the small visualization.
As for its characteristics, according to the translation by Liu Qiu:
one should paint an image of Avalokiteśvara.
Now, paint a thirty-two-petaled lotus flower in full bloom; upon its central platform,
depict the Holy Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva of the Wish-Fulfilling Wheel (Cintāmaṇicakra),
facing west and seated in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*).
His countenance is radiant and joyful, and his body possesses the mark of golden color.
On his head he wears a jeweled crown in which there is an emanated Buddha and Bodhisattva;
in his left hand he holds a blossoming flower, upon whose center a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*) should be painted.
His right hand is in the gesture of preaching the Dharma.
Adorned with exquisite celestial garments, pearl earrings, bracelets, and bangles,
and embellished with necklaces of the seven precious gems, his body emits manifold rays of light.
The practitioner, relying on these noble signs, should maintain mindfulness and observe them,
knowing that these signs arise from the mind’s conceptualization and are,
like flowers in the sky, fundamentally non-existent.
These appearances and the mind are fundamentally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of Avalokiteśvara.
As illusory flowers in the sky, they are provisional; as being originally non-existent, they are empty.
This wondrous essence is the Middle—thus the three truths are perfectly interfused.
It is neither one nor different, and cannot be grasped through conceptual thought.
Not only is the mark of the Sage thus, but all his teachings are likewise so.
This is truly because the nature of sentient beings inherently possesses all dharmas.
Therefore, they are able to arise in accordance with conditions.
Because Bodhisattvas cultivate and realize all dharmas,
they are able to manifest through the universal gate.
Although all phenomena are distinct, they are identical within emptiness.

If there were only distinction and no identity, the principle of responsive resonance would be lost; if there were only identity and no distinction, the phenomenon of responsive resonance would be lost. To lose the principle...
They are as incompatible as ice and fire.
One who errs regarding affairs is like an echo that cannot be summoned.
When both the facts and the principles are complete, the response is then realized.
Furthermore, it should be understood that the dharma of the three truths is precisely the meaning elucidated by the vidyā-mantra;
therefore, Yi Jing translated it as "Unobstructed."
Regarding the *Avalokiteśvara-padma-cintāmaṇi-cakra-rāja-dhāraṇī*,
the term "unobstructed" refers to the Bodhisattva possessing the wisdom of the three truths and being free from the obstructions of the three delusions.
Avalokiteśvara observes sentient beings with this wisdom and thereby attains sovereignty.
This is because the person who can speak [the mantra] bestows life upon the mantra being spoken.
The lotus flower bears fruit upon its birth;
this is an analogy for the virtues of the Dharmakāya, which are inherently and fully possessed from the beginning.
The "wish-fulfilling" refers to the wish-fulfilling jewel.
The Sūtra says:
"It rains exquisite treasures, like the wish-fulfilling tree and the wish-fulfilling jewel."
The quality of liberation is like that which can give rise to all phenomena;
the precious wheel possesses the power to subdue and conquer,
which is analogous to the quality of prajñā, which can penetrate and dismantle all phenomena.
Furthermore, the lotus flower emerging from the water, free from defilement and pure, is a metaphor for *prajñā* (wisdom).
Its fragrant calyx is a metaphor for *vimukti* (liberation), and the inherently perfect sphere of the pearl is a metaphor for the *dharmakāya* (dharma-body).
Its color is brilliant and pure, symbolizing *prajñā*;
its substance is precious, like the *dharmakāya*;
and its function of revolving is like *vimukti*.
Since each of these three types possesses three meanings, they are illustrated by way of the three virtues (*triguṇa*).
To cite one is to possess all three; thus, "three" is itself "one."
Because it expresses this meaning,
it is called "King" (rāja), as it universally encompasses all phenomena and transcends them all.
It obstructs the evils of the nine realms and maintains the goodness of the Buddha-realm.
Therefore, it is called a dhāraṇī.
Furthermore, Śikṣānanda translated it as "Secret Treasury Divine Mantra.
If it were not the dharma of the three virtues and the three truths, it would not be so.
How can one peacefully accept this name?
When a bodhisattva practices for themselves, they do so solely within emptiness;
when transforming others, they follow conventional designations to reach sentient beings.
Sentient beings undergo transformation within the provisional;
even when transformation reaches its limit, it exists only within emptiness.
Thus, the *Awakening of Faith* states: "If one is separated from the karmic consciousness, there is neither seeing nor appearance."
Because the Dharma-bodies of all Buddhas possess no such things as self or other,
nor do they perceive one another through physical forms;
thus has it been briefly explained.
If you wish to understand the characteristics [of practice] in detail, you should seek the *Yùquán Zhǐguān* (Jade Spring Calming and Contemplation). **Third:

Rites of Worship and Praise** With all reverence, with a single mind, I pay homage to the Three Jewels—Eternal, Abiding, and Present—in the ten directions. Having paid homage, I kneel long and hold the incense burner, burning incense: "I now, according to the Dharma, reverently offer this incense and flowers."
I make offerings to all the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, throughout the boundless Dharma-realm of the ten directions;

to the twelve divisions of the scriptures; and to the noble assemblies of the Three Vehicles. Having visualized holding the incense burner and offering flowers, which are then dispersed, one further says: "The offerings have been completed. Then, with all reverence, rise and perform one prostration, bowing deeply while praising as follows:
Within the Tathāgatagarbha lies the true Dharma-treasure; according to the dispositions of sentient beings, it manifests and flows forth.
This is the sublime mantra proclaimed by the Great Compassionate One, the Holy Avalokiteśvara, known as the Cintāmaṇicakra, which causes all [afflictions] to be utterly extinguished.
It can also accomplish immeasurable sufferings and calamities, as well as all that is sought;
for this reason, Śākyamuni has earnestly praised and extolled the various dhāraṇīs.
Regarding those who are equal to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), I now set forth my intent.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to our Teacher, Śākyamuni Bhagavān.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to Amitābha Bhagavān of the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, throughout the Dharma-realm of the ten directions.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Unobstructed Sovereign Lotus Wish-Fulfilling Jewel Wheel King Dhāraṇī.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the twelve divisions of the sūtras throughout the dharma-realm of the ten directions.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the Great Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, the Vidyārājas who fulfill all wishes and intentions.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the noble assembly of the three vehicles throughout the ten directions and the entire dharma realm. The fourth scripture states:
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Bhagavān, I now possess a great dhāraṇī mantra,
namely: the Unobstructed Avalokiteśvara,
the Lotus Wish-Fulfilling Jewel Wheel King."
"O World-Honored One of Great Compassion, if you would grant me leave to speak, this is most rare and extraordinary:
that regarding all matters sought, one may obtain fulfillment and benefit according to one's heart."
"I shall, relying on the Buddha's majestic power, bestow [this] upon sentient beings.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One praised the Bodhisattva, saying:
"So it is, so it is! You are indeed able to have compassion for all classes of sentient beings."
"I shall protect you.
Having received the Buddha's permission, the Bodhisattva, his heart overflowing with compassionate vows,
immediately spoke this mantra before the Buddha:

Namo buddhāya. Namo dharmāya. Namo saṃghāya. Namo Avalokiteśvarāya bodhisattvāya mahāsattvāya mahākāruṇikāya. Tadyathā: Oṃ cakravarti cindāmaṇi mahāpraḍume ruru ruru tiṣṭha ṭhaṭha kala akaliśaya hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. This is called the Root Mantra. Oṃ padma cindāmaṇi ṭhaṭha hūṃ. This is called the Great Heart Mantra. Oṃ varada pradumye hūṃ. This is called the Close-Heart Mantra. At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara...
Having spoken this dhāraṇī,
the great earth shook in six ways,
and the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and others [were moved].
All the celestial palaces likewise rotated and became disorienting;
all the evil Māras who acted as obstacles saw their own palaces erupting in flames, none of whom failed to be struck with terror.
Even down to those sentient beings suffering within the hells, may they all be freed from suffering and attain rebirth in the heavens.

Fifth Repentance and Vow: For the sake of the four debts of gratitude and all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm of the three realms of existence, may they all vow to sever and eliminate the three obstacles.
I take refuge and repent; with a sincere heart I repent.
I, the bhikṣu [Name], take refuge in the eternally abiding Triple Gem of the ten directions:
Śākyamuni Buddha, Amitābha Buddha, and the Holy Avalokiteśvara, who possesses great compassion.
I pray that you will arise with compassion and act as my witness:
for the sake of all sentient beings in the dharma-realm,
the nature of mind from beginningless time is like a mani jewel.
The self-nature is pure and its divine function is primordial; it constitutes the single secret treasury of all Tathāgatas.
Yet, through the movement of deluded thoughts, there is illusory existence and saṃsāra, wherein one undergoes various torments within birth and death.
That is to say, regarding the karma of the four grave offenses, the five heinous crimes, and the ten evil deeds committed and accumulated in the past and present,
one is destined to fall into the suffering of the Avīci Hell.
Due to such evil karma, one is currently beset by all manner of illnesses and various calamities in this very body.
As extensively described in the sūtras regarding the various causes and conditions of evil,
I now respectfully follow the instructions of the Greatly Compassionate Holy Avalokiteśvara and recite and uphold this Wish-Fulfilling Jewel Wheel.
May such karmic obstructions be extinguished and eliminated.
May all that is wished for among the hundreds of thousands of matters be fulfilled.
I only pray that the Bodhisattva will accept my repentance.
I bestow upon those who seek from me the wish-fulfilling jewel (*maṇi*),
raining down all manner of precious treasures— the worldly and supramundane provisions of merit and wisdom—
so that all may have their hearts' desires fulfilled without exception.
Until the end of their natural lifespan, they shall not enter a womb; instead,
they will be born by transformation from a lotus in the World of Ultimate Bliss,
where they will behold the true physical bodies of Amitābha Buddha and Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
Having heard the sublime sound of the Dharma and realized the nature of universal penetration,
they then manifest universally through the Gate of All Doors to benefit sentient beings,
leading them all out of worldly toil and affliction to together achieve the Wisdom of All Modes.

Homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions. Homage to the Dharma of the ten directions. Homage to the Sangha of the ten directions. Homage to our Original Teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha. Homage to Amitābha Buddha. Homage to the Cintāmaṇicakra Dhāraṇī. Homage to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. Homage to Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva. Homage to all the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who have fulfilled their vows. (Recite this three times or seven times.)
